hero.filename: Early Autumn in the Amazon Basin (MODIS 2026-03-24).jpg
hero.caption:
On March 22, 2026, the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) on NASA’s Terra satellite acquired this true-color image of a nearly cloud-free early autumn day in South America’s Amazon Basin.
Winding rivers, some tan and some dark, cut through the heart of the deep green Amazon rainforest. As the rivers course through the landscape, they help create a wide variety of habitats, such as marshes or floodplains, each supporting its own array of species. Taken together, the Amazon rainforest and the river system remains the most biologically diverse place on Earth, hosting millions of known species.
This image highlights the intricate river system of the Amazon Basin. The Rio Negro flows from the northwest to the southeast and is filled with dark water. The Rio Negro flows into the mud-colored Solimões River (also known as the upper Amazon River) just east of the city of Manaus, where they form the Amazon River. The Amazon itself is also filled with muddy sediment and appears distinctly tan.

Haze covers the western portion of the Amazon Basin visible in this image. Most of these fires are not visible in this portion of the rainforest. According to a wider view available on the NASA Worldview App, most of smoke appears to come from fires in the northwest, especially in Venezuela.

images.caption:
A piranha or piraña (/pɪˈrɑːnjə/, /pɪˈrænjə/, or /pɪˈrɑːnə/; Portuguese: [piˈɾɐ̃ɲɐ] or [piˈɾɐ̃j̃ɐ], Spanish: [piˈɾaɲa]) is one of a number of freshwater fish in the family Serrasalmidae,[1] or the subfamily Serrasalminae within the tetra family, Characidae[2] in order Characiformes. These fish inhabit South American rivers, floodplains, lakes and reservoirs. Although often described as extremely predatory and mainly feeding on fish, their dietary habits vary extensively, and they will also take plant material,[3] leading to their classification as omnivorous.
Source: Wikipedia

images.caption:
On September 27, 2023, the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) on NASA’s Terra satellite acquired a true-color image of a nearly cloud-free day over the Amazon Basin.
Centered on the state of Amazonas, Brazil, the image captures the Amazon River and its many tributaries winding through luxuriant growth of rainforest. The Amazon River appears muddy in many areas, where it carries sediment from the surrounding lands, including as far as the mountains of Peru, where the earliest tributaries rise.

The clear skies and relatively narrow width of the rivers are clues that show that this image was acquired well into the dry season, which runs from June to November. The driest month in the Amazon Basin is August, with an average rainfall is about 2 inches (5 cm). In contrast, rainfall from May – December is often more than 8 inches (20 cm) per month, with a total annual rainfall averaging between 6 – 10 feet (1.3 to 3 meters).

images.caption: A bioluminescent bug. We found this bug during a night expedition in the Amazon rainforest, while looking for bioluminescence.  It had a bright blue glow to it. It is remarkable, because blue bioluminescence is extremely rare in land organisms, only found in one other species, in South America. The bug was killed by a little spider, as we tried to capture it. The bug might be a whole new species, yet unknown to science. Night expedition was a part of a volunteering programme at IPBio, (Instituto de pesquisas da biodiversidade).
